subject: Clarify how token metering and minimums apply to committed discounts
messages:
From: Daniel Weber <daniel.weber@acme.com>
To: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@acme.com
Date: Wed, 28 Jul 2027 09:14:00 -0700
Subject: Questions on metering: rounding & minimums for long transcripts

Hi Rafael,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — the team liked the latency profile. Procurement has a couple of nitty-gritty questions before we sign the SOW:

1) How do you meter tokens for streaming responses that exceed our pinned context? For example, if a single user session produces a 30k token transcript (chat history + new output), do you split billing across multiple context segments or charge on the aggregated tokens?

2) Do you round partial token usage up to the nearest token unit, or do you aggregate across a billing window? Is there a minimum charge per request? Our legal team is concerned about micro-requests causing unpredictable monthly spend.

3) For our committed discount (we're looking at 1.2M tokens/month committed), how do minimums and rounding interact with committed vs overage usage? If we commit but usage is bursty, does the platform smooth to the commit, or do burst spikes push us into higher overage tiers?

Can you provide a simple worked example that we can include with the procurement paperwork?

Appreciate it — copying procurement.

Best,
Daniel
Daniel Weber
Sr. Technical Program Manager — AI Platform
ACME Corporation

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.com>
To: Daniel Weber <daniel.weber@acme.com>
Cc: marissa.cole@redwood.com, karthik.iyer@redwood.com, procurement@acme.com
Date: Thu, 29 Jul 2027 08:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Questions on metering: rounding & minimums for long transcripts

Hi Daniel — thanks for the clear questions. High-level answers below; Marissa from billing and Karthik from pricing will add the precise math and invoice examples.

Short answers:
- We meter every token consumed for generation and context ingestion (same as standard token models). For very long sessions we use context "windowing" during serving: the runtime slices the request into contiguous context segments for execution, but billing is for total tokens processed (no hidden multiplication).
- Rounding is done at the token level, but we perform aggregation per-minute per-customer for smoothing before final billing. That means many tiny requests will be summed rather than each rounding separately, which reduces micro-charge noise.
- For committed discounts: the commit is applied to aggregated usage in the billing cycle after smoothing. Bursty spikes still count toward usage and apply to overage if you exceed the commit. We do not automatically move you into a higher committed tier mid-cycle; overages are billed at the agreed overage rate.

I'll let Marissa and Karthik post a worked example (short spreadsheet) and call out where minimums apply vs per-request floors.

Thanks,
Rafael
Rafael Mendes
Enterprise Sales — Redwood Inference

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Daniel Weber <daniel.weber@acme.com>, Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@acme.com, karthik.iyer@redwood.com
Date: Fri, 30 Jul 2027 10:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Questions on metering: rounding & minimums for long transcripts

Hi Daniel — putting the billing rules in plain language and then a small numeric example. Attaching a sample invoice that mirrors the example (sample-invoice-ACME-July.xlsx).

Rules:
- Token unit: We count raw model tokens (the same tokenizer across all billing). Partial tokens are not a separate billable unit — tokenization returns integer token counts.
- Per-request floor: For non-streaming generation calls, there is a 1-token effective minimum (so a 0.3-token hypothetical would round up to 1 token — practical impact is negligible).
- Aggregation window: We aggregate tokens per customer over a one-minute rolling window before rounding to minimize micro-request noise. So 100 requests each of 0.6 tokens in the same minute will be billed as 60 tokens (after aggregation) rather than 100 tokens.
- Context windowing: For requests that exceed a single model context length, the runtime executes as multiple inference passes. Billing equals the sum of tokens submitted for encoding (context) plus tokens generated. We do not double-count cached KV entries — KV cache hits are not billed again for the same session when enabled.
- Minimum monthly commitment application: If you commit to a monthly token volume, your monthly invoice will apply the committed discount against the smoothed aggregated usage first. If usage < commit, you're billed for the committed quantity (the minimum). If usage > commit, the excess is billed at the overage rate per the SOW.

Short worked example (numbers):
- Commit: 1,200,000 tokens/month at $0.0010/token (committed rate)
- Overage rate: $0.0014/token
- Week with bursts: Day A: 1,400,000 tokens (peak day), remaining days total 600,000 tokens — month total 2,000,000 tokens.
Billing: 1,200,000 tokens at committed rate = $1,200.00
         800,000 tokens overage at $0.0014 = $1,120.00
         Total = $2,320.00 (plus any agreed credits/discount adjustments)

Notes:
- The per-minute aggregation reduces micro-request rounding noise; it does not change the total tokens consumed for long transcripts.
- If you enable session-level KV caching, you may materially reduce tokens billed for repeated context reads — we'll include guidance in the SOW appendix on enabling and sizing session cache for your workload.

Let me know if you want a variant that shows per-request floors (we can simulate conservative rounding) or an example with embeddings mixed in.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Billing & Revenue Operations — Redwood Inference

Attachment: sample-invoice-ACME-July.xlsx (spreadsheet: breakdown by day, commit applied, taxes placeholder)

Marissa — thanks, that helps a lot. A couple quick follow-ups so procurement can sign:

- Can you confirm that the per-minute aggregation is tenant-scoped (i.e., across all API keys for ACME) and not per API key? We authenticate across multiple services so this matters.
- For KV caching: is the cache TTL per session (user) or per conversation id? We need to know whether cross-service cache hits are possible for our microservices architecture.

If you can add those two clarifications to the sample invoice spreadsheet and re-upload, procurement will be comfortable moving forward.

Thanks,
Daniel

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
To: Daniel Weber <daniel.weber@acme.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@acme.com
Date: Mon, 2 Aug 2027 16:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Questions on metering: rounding & minimums for long transcripts

Hi Daniel — quick clarifications from the pricing/engineering side:

1) Aggregation scope: The one-minute aggregation is tenant-scoped (all API keys and subprojects under the tenant ID are aggregated together). We do not aggregate across customers. We'll add a note to the SOW appendix so your infra team sees the exact tenant ID used for aggregation.

2) KV cache semantics: Session KV cache is per-conversation id by default. We offer two modes:
   - session-scoped (default): cache keyed by conversation/session id; best for UI chat apps where a single session reuses context.
   - tenant-shared cache (opt-in enterprise setting): cache keyed at tenant level to allow multiple services to share KV hits — this can reduce billing but requires coordinating TTL and access controls.

I've updated the sample-invoice worksheet with a toggle column showing typical token reduction from tenant-shared caching vs session-scoped caching and re-uploaded as sample-invoice-ACME-July.xlsx (v2). I also included a short tab that simulates per-minute aggregation effects on high-frequency micro-requests.

If you'd like, we can schedule a 30-minute call with our solutions architect to run these numbers against a sample traffic trace.

Cheers,
Karthik Iyer
Pricing & Platform Economics — Redwood Inference
